claim: Grid cells were discovered in medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) by Hafting et al., 2005.
source: The discovery of grid cells in medial entorhinal cortex (MEC; Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Grid cells are organized into discrete modules.
source: The organization of grid cells into discrete modules (Stensola et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stensola et al., 2012 and Gu et al., 2018.

claim: Grid properties (grid spacing and orientation) are clustered within module, but not between modules.
source: The organization of grid cells into discrete modules (Stensola et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2018), with grid properties (grid spacing and orientation) clustered within module, but not between modules
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stensola et al., 2012 and Gu et al., 2018.

claim: Grid modules increase in size and spacing along the dorsal-ventral axis of MEC by discontinuous jumps of a near constant ratio.
source: the increasing size and spacing of grid modules along the dorsal-ventral axis of MEC, by discontinuous jumps of a near constant ratio
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the text discussing grid module organization.

claim: The increasing size and spacing of grid modules has been argued to be optimal for encoding local spatial information when grid cell activity across all modules is integrated together.
source: the increasing size and spacing of grid modules along the dorsal-ventral axis of MEC, by discontinuous jumps of a near constant ratio, has been argued to be optimal for encoding local spatial information (Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015) when grid cell activity across all modules is integrated together (Fiete et al., 2008; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Mathis et al., 2012a; Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015; Fiete et al., 2008; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Mathis et al., 2012a.

claim: Individual neurons in hippocampus receive inputs from only a portion of the dorsal-ventral axis of MEC.
source: This is despite the fact that the individual neurons in hippocampus, a downstream target of the MEC, receive inputs from only a portion of the dorsal-ventral axis (van Strien et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Strien et al., 2009.

claim: The modularity of the grid system has been proposed to simplify the wiring necessary for generating continuous attractor dynamics.
source: The modularity of the grid system has also been proposed to simplify the wiring necessary for generating continuous attractor dynamics (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Guanella and Verschure, 2006; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Couey et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Guanella and Verschure, 2006; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Couey et al., 2013.

claim: Continuous attractor dynamics is a computational mechanism theorized to underlie grid cells function that enjoys considerable experimental support.
source: a computational mechanism theorized to underlie grid cells function that enjoys considerable experimental support (Yoon et al., 2013; Dunn et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2018; Gardner et al., 2019; Trettel et al., 2019; Gardner et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yoon et al., 2013; Dunn et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2018; Gardner et al., 2019; Trettel et al., 2019; Gardner et al., 2022.

claim: Much prior theoretical work has made the assumption that grid cell properties are identical, up to a phase shift, within a single module.
source: Much of this prior theoretical work has made the additional assumption that grid cell properties are identical, up to a phase shift, within a single module (Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Mathis et al., 2012a; Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015; Dorrell et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Mathis et al., 2012a; Wei et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015; Dorrell et al., 2023.

claim: The distributions of measured orientation and spacing show non-zero variability.
source: However, as experimentalists have been aware, the distributions of measured orientation and spacing show non-zero variability (Stensola et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2013; Gardner et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stensola et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2013; Gardner et al., 2022.

claim: No characterization of the degree and robustness of variability in grid properties within individual modules has been performed.
source: Despite the fundamental way in which grid cell function has been informed by their modular organization, to the best of our knowledge, no characterization of the degree and robustness of variability in grid properties within individual modules has been performed.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: When all grid cells in a module have the same grid orientation and spacing, the joint population activity has a translational invariance that persists, even as larger populations of grid cells are considered.
source: In particular, when all grid cells in a module have the same grid orientation and spacing, the joint population activity has a translational invariance that persists, even as larger populations of grid cells are considered (Figure 1, 'Fixed grid properties within module').
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and logical inference about the properties of grid cells with identical spacing and orientation.

claim: When grid cells within a module have variability in their grid orientation and spacing, over a finite area, the translational invariance of the population activity is broken.
source: In contrast, if grid cells within a module have variability in their grid orientation and spacing, then – over a finite area – the translational invariance of the population activity is broken.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the effects of variability in grid properties.

claim: When grid cells have variable grid properties, distinct patterns of population activity emerge in distinct locations of space.
source: In such a case, distinct patterns of population activity emerge in distinct locations of space (Figure 1, 'Variable grid properties within module').
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 showing distinct patterns.

claim: The analyzed data comes from recent state-of-the-art MEC electrophysiological recordings made publicly available by Gardner et al., 2022.
source: In this paper, we perform detailed analysis of recent state-of-the-art MEC electrophysiological recordings, which were made publicly available (Gardner et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2022.

claim: There is evidence for small, but robust, variability in grid orientation and spacing within individual modules.
source: We characterize the variability of grid orientation and spacing within individual modules and find evidence for small, but robust, variability.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis performed in the manuscript.

claim: Grid property variability is present whether a single value of grid orientation and spacing is assigned to each grid cell, or whether grid distortion is taken into account by considering three grid orientations and spacings independently.
source: This variability is present whether a single value of grid orientation and spacing is assigned to each grid cell, or whether grid distortion (Derdikman et al., 2009; Krupic et al., 2015) is taken into account by considering three grid orientations and spacings independently.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis in the manuscript and citations to Derdikman et al., 2009; Krupic et al., 2015.

claim: Normative recurrent neural network (RNN) models of grid cells show the presence of comparable variability to that found in experimental data.
source: Performing similar analysis on recent normative recurrent neural network (RNN) models of grid cells (Sorscher et al., 2019), we find the presence of comparable variability.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNN models and citation to Sorscher et al., 2019.

claim: The presence of comparable variability in RNN models provides another possible explanation for why these RNN models have been found to capture MEC grid cell response profiles.
source: This provides another possible explanation for why these RNN models have been found to capture MEC grid cell response profiles (Nayebi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results and citation to Nayebi et al., 2021.

claim: Grid property variability at a similar degree as present in the analyzed data leads to lower decoding error of local space when using the activity of a single module.
source: We find that the variability in grid cell orientation and spacing, at a similar degree as present in the data we analyze, leads to lower decoding error of local space when using the activity of a single module.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation experiments with synthetic grid cell populations.

claim: The within-cell variability of grid orientation and spacing is significantly smaller than the between-cell variability.
source: We find that the distribution, across 100 random shuffles of the data into two halves, of within-cell variability of grid orientation and spacing is more concentrated around 0 than the between-cell variability (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The average grid field width does not significantly affect the between-cell variability.
source: We perform a number of control analyses to confirm that our results are robust, finding that: (1) the average grid field width does not significantly affect the between-cell variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amount of between-cell variability does not change significantly across the recording duration.
source: (2) the amount of between-cell variability does not change significantly across the recording duration (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The between-cell variability is not significantly impacted by the boundaries of the arena.
source: (3) the between-cell variability is not significantly impacted by the boundaries of the arena (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The amount of between-cell variability is not driven by the presence of conjunctive cells.
source: (4) the amount of between-cell variability is not driven by the presence of cells that have both head direction and grid cell like tuning 'conjunctive' cells (Sargolini et al., 2006; Figure 3—figure supplement 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6 and citation to Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: Grid properties are significantly more robust within-cell than between-cell when restricting analysis to each axis separately.
source: The results again demonstrate that grid properties are significantly more robust within-cell than between-cell (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: For each axis, the average between-cell variability for every cell was significantly higher than the average within-cell variability.
source: For each axis, the average between-cell variability for every cell was significantly higher than the average within-cell variability (Figure 4C and D), as reported by the Wilcoxon-Signed-Rank Test for orientation (p < 0.001, for all three axes) and for spacing (p < 0.001, for all three axes).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: RNN models trained to perform path integration develop grid responses with a distribution of grid spacing and orientation.
source: We find that the RNNs develop grid responses with a distribution of grid spacing and orientation (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A-D), much like the neural data we analyzed (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A-D.

claim: Changing the sparsity of the recurrent layer by increasing the strength of weight decay regularization reduces the variability in RNN models.
source: Changing the sparsity of the recurrent layer by increasing the strength of weight decay regularization reduces the variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 7E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7E, F.

claim: Grid cells in the same grid module do not have a single grid spacing and orientation, but instead have a restricted range of values around the module mean.
source: Taken together, our analysis of large-scale MEC recordings demonstrates that grid cells in the same grid module do not have a single grid spacing and orientation, but instead have a restricted range of values around the module mean.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall analysis of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The variability in grid properties is a robust feature that cannot be explained by noise from the recording or fitting procedures.
source: This property is a robust feature that cannot be explained by noise from the recording or fitting procedures and emerges in existing normative models of MEC.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis comparing within- and between-cell variability.

claim: Variability in grid properties similar to what is quantified in the real data can be sufficient to accurately decode information of local space in noisy synthetic populations of grid cells.
source: We find, in noisy synthetic populations of grid cells, that a level of variability in grid properties similar to what is quantified in the real data can be sufficient to accurately decode information of local space (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The benefit of grid property variability for decoding is increased with larger numbers of grid cells in the population.
source: This benefit is increased with larger numbers of grid cells in the population (Figure 6D)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The benefit of grid property variability for decoding is observed over a range of values for the underlying variability.
source: and is observed over a range of values for the underlying variability (Figure 6F)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The improvement in decoding was most pronounced in modules with small grid spacing.
source: We find that the improvement was most pronounced in modules with small grid spacing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Larger modules can see a decrease in decoding error for amounts of variability consistent with what was found in the analyzed data.
source: although larger modules can see a decrease in decoding error for amounts of variability consistent with was was found in the analyzed data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Heterogeneity in maximal firing rates across individual grid fields has been recently found.
source: We note that our results are additionally aligned with recent findings of heterogeneity in maximal firing rates across individual grid fields (Diehl et al., 2017; Ismakov et al., 2017; Dunn et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Diehl et al., 2017; Ismakov et al., 2017; Dunn et al., 2017.

claim: Grid sheering has been recently found.
source: and grid sheering (Derdikman et al., 2009; Krupic et al., 2015; Ginosar et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Derdikman et al., 2009; Krupic et al., 2015; Ginosar et al., 2023.

claim: Even in the absence of heterogeneity in maximal firing rates and grid sheering, individual grid modules may encode considerably more local spatial information than previously believed.
source: Our work further demonstrates that, even in the absence of these perturbations, individual grid modules may encode considerably more local spatial information than previously believed.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the decoding analysis.

claim: Models of the formation of orientation maps in visual cortex have demonstrated that slight angular offsets of retinal mosaics can generate complex patterns similar to those found in visual cortex orientation maps.
source: Finally, models of the formation of orientation maps in visual cortex have demonstrated that slight angular offsets of retinal mosaics, along which retinal receptive fields are organized, can generate complex patterns (Paik and Ringach, 2011) similar to those found in visual cortex orientation maps (Blasdel and Salama, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paik and Ringach, 2011 and Blasdel and Salama, 1986.

claim: Grid cells in MEC may take advantage of a similar computational principle as orientation maps in visual cortex, suggesting that mosaic patterns might be a broadly utilized feature of neural coding.
source: Our results indicate that grid cells in MEC may take advantage of a similar computational principle, suggesting that mosaic patterns might be a broadly utilized feature of neural coding (Smith and Smith, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the results and citation to Smith and Smith, 2011.

claim: The analyzed data set represents an advance in the ability to simultaneously record from tens to hundreds of putative grid cells across grid modules.
source: While the data set we analyzed (Gardner et al., 2022) represents an advance in the ability to simultaneously record from tens to hundreds of putative grid cells, across grid modules, the MEC remains a challenging brain region to access for large-scale neurophysiological experiments.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the data set and citation to Gardner et al., 2022.

claim: With conservative inclusion criteria, only 420 grid cells were included in the analysis.
source: Indeed, with our conservative inclusion criteria, we were ultimately limited by having only 420 grid cells included in our analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on the data analysis performed.

claim: The decoding analysis made the simplifying assumption of independent Poisson noise for neural activity.
source: Our decoding analysis, while demonstrating the possibility that variability in grid properties can be used by individual grid modules to enhance the encoding of local spatial information, made several simplifying assumptions, including: (1) independent Poisson noise for neural activity
evidence: The claim describes a methodological assumption made in the analysis.

claim: The decoding analysis made the simplifying assumption of linear decoding.
source: (2) linear decoding
evidence: The claim describes a methodological assumption made in the analysis.

claim: The decoding analysis made the simplifying assumption of normal distribution of grid properties.
source: (3) normal distribution of grid properties
evidence: The claim describes a methodological assumption made in the analysis.

claim: Comparison to real data showed that the assumptions made in the decoding analysis are reasonable.
source: Although comparison to real data showed that these assumptions are reasonable (Figure 6E)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Continuous attractor network models of grid cells make use of the assumption that all the grid cells in a given module have the same grid orientation and spacing to simplify the network connectivity.
source: However, these models make use of the assumption that all the grid cells in a given module have the same grid orientation and spacing to simplify the network connectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of continuous attractor network models.

claim: By assuming equal grid orientation and spacing, it becomes possible to arrange grid cells in a two-dimensional space spanned by their phases (i.e. a 'neural sheet').
source: In particular, by assuming equal grid orientation and spacing, it becomes possible to arrange grid cells in a two-dimensional space spanned by their phases (i.e. a 'neural sheet' Burak and Fiete, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of continuous attractor network models and citation to Burak and Fiete, 2009.

claim: The data set analyzed was found by others to provide strong support for the basic predictions of continuous attractor networks (i.e. toroidal topology of the activity manifold).
source: As the data set we analyzed was found by others to provide strong support for the basic predictions of continuous attractor networks (i.e. toroidal topology of the activity manifold; Gardner et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2022.

claim: The authors do not view their results as directly challenging continuous attractor network models.
source: we do not view our results as directly challenging these models
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement of the authors' interpretation.

claim: The RNN models investigated are explicitly trained to perform path integration and achieve highly accurate performance.
source: That the RNN models we investigate (Figure 3—figure supplement 7) are explicitly trained to perform path integration (and achieve highly accurate performance Sorscher et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 7 and citation to Sorscher et al., 2023.

claim: The authors hypothesize that the degree in variability of grid spacing and orientation may strike a balance between being small enough to keep the continuous attractor network structure stable, but large enough to enable encoding of local information of space.
source: We hypothesize that the degree in variability of grid spacing and orientation may strike a balance between being small enough to keep the continuous attractor network structure stable, but large enough to enable encoding of local information of space.
evidence: The claim is an explicit hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: One hypothesis for the source of heterogeneity in grid cell properties is that it could be driven by 'defects' in the specific connectivity pattern that is needed for a continuous attractor.
source: One hypothesis is that this could be driven by 'defects' in the specific connectivity pattern that is needed for a continuous attractor.
evidence: The claim is an explicit hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: Smaller weight decay (and thus, denser connectivity between units) in RNNs led to greater variability in grid properties.
source: We find that smaller weight decay (and thus, denser connectivity between units) led to greater variability in grid properties (Figure 3—figure supplement 7E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7E, F.

claim: Increasing the weight decay (and thus, enforcing sparser connectivity) in RNNs led to a reduction of grid property variability.
source: Increasing the weight decay (and thus, enforcing sparser connectivity) led to a reduction of grid property variability (Figure 3—figure supplement 7E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7E, F.

claim: The heterogeneity in grid properties observed may be due to 'non-perfect' connectivity.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the heterogeneity in grid properties we observe may be due to 'non-perfect' connectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RNN analysis.

claim: The coupling between hippocampus and MEC has been shown to lead to variability in grid field firing rates.
source: Alternatively, the coupling between hippocampus and MEC, which has been shown to lead to variability in grid field firing rates (as experimentally observed; Dunn et al., 2017; Agmon and Burak, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2017 and Agmon and Burak, 2020.

claim: A previous computational model that learned grid cells from place cell input using non-negative principal component analysis has shown that place field width affects grid cell orientation and spacing.
source: In particular, a previous computational model that learned grid cells from place cell input, using non-negative principal component analysis, has shown that place field width affects grid cell orientation and spacing (Dordek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dordek et al., 2016.

claim: Heterogeneity in the spatial coding properties of place cells has been found along the transverse axis of CA3.
source: Heterogeneity in the spatial coding properties of place cells has been found along the transverse axis of CA3 (Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Redman et al., 2022b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Redman et al., 2022b.

claim: The place-to-grid cell computational model has a linear relationship between place field width and grid spacing.
source: Further, it was shown that this place-to-grid cell computational model has a linear relationship between place field width and grid spacing, and a non-monotonic relationship between place field width and grid orientation (Dordek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dordek et al., 2016.

claim: The place-to-grid cell computational model has a non-monotonic relationship between place field width and grid orientation.
source: Further, it was shown that this place-to-grid cell computational model has a linear relationship between place field width and grid spacing, and a non-monotonic relationship between place field width and grid orientation (Dordek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dordek et al., 2016.

claim: The relationships in the place-to-grid cell model may explain why stronger average variability in grid spacing than grid orientation was found.
source: These may explain why we find stronger average variability in grid spacing than grid orientation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference connecting the model properties to the observed data.

claim: Grid cells have been reported to maintain their grid spacing and orientation across exposures to new environments, while undergoing a change in their grid phase.
source: First, given that grid cells have been reported to maintain their grid spacing and orientation across exposures to new environments, while undergoing a change in their grid phase (Fyhn et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fyhn et al., 2007 and Yoon et al., 2013.

claim: Recent work on hippocampal place field drift has demonstrated that there is a significant change in the place field location across time, especially in CA1.
source: And second, recent work on hippocampal place field drift (Mankin et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2021) has demonstrated that there is a significant change in the place field location across time, especially in CA1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mankin et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2021.

claim: One possible source of place field drift is the reported instability of dendritic spines on the apical dendrites of CA1 place cells.
source: One possible source of this phenomenon is the reported instability of dendritic spines on the apical dendrites of CA1 place cells (Mizrahi et al., 2004; Attardo et al., 2015; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Redman et al., 2022b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mizrahi et al., 2004; Attardo et al., 2015; Pfeiffer et al., 2018; Redman et al., 2022b.

claim: Three male Long Evans rats (Rats Q, R, and S) were implanted with Neuropixels silicon probes.
source: Three male rats (Long Evans – Rats Q, R, and S) were implanted with Neuropixels silicon probes (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and is supported by citations to Jun et al., 2017 and Steinmetz et al., 2021.

claim: The Neuropixels probes were targeted at the MEC-parasubiculum region.
source: These probes were targeted at the MEC-parasubiculum region and the surgery was performed as described previously (Gardner et al., 2019; Steinmetz et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and is supported by citations to Gardner et al., 2019 and Steinmetz et al., 2021.

claim: In the recordings analyzed, the rats foraged for randomly dispersed corn puffs in a 1.5 × 1.5m² square open field arena, with walls of height 50 cm.
source: In the recordings analyzed, the rats foraged for randomly dispersed corn puffs in a 1.5 × 1.5m2 square open field arena, with walls of height 50 cm.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: All procedures in the original study were approved by the Norwegian Food and Safety Authority and done in accordance with the Norwegian Animal Welfare Act and the European Convention for the Protection of Vertebrate Animals used for Experimental and Other Scientific Purposes.
source: All procedures in the original study were approved by the Norwegian Food and Safety Authority and done in accordance with the Norwegian Animal Welfare Act and the European Convention for the Protection of Vertebrate Animals used for Experimental and Other Scientific Purposes.
